blocks.x: [Projectile non-bilious vomiting / Rule out hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.]
Targeted real-time high-frequency linear ultrasound of the gastric outlet and pyloric canal, supplemented by a survey of the solid abdominal organs and pelvis.
Liver, Gallbladder, Pancreas & Spleen: Normal size and echogenicity for age; no focal lesion or biliary dilatation.
Kidneys & Bladder: Normal bilateral kidneys without hydronephrosis. Urinary bladder is unremarkable.
Bowel & Peritoneum: Normal mesenteric vascular orientation. No intussusception, bowel dilatation, or free peritoneal fluid.
[Non-bilious projectile vomiting / Rule out hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.]
Real-time grayscale ultrasound of the upper abdomen, pyloric canal, and general abdominopelvic organs using high-frequency linear and pediatric curvilinear transducers.
Normal hepatic size and homogeneous echogenicity. Gallbladder is unremarkable without biliary dilatation. Visualized pancreas and spleen are normal.
Normal bilateral pediatric kidneys without hydronephrosis. Urinary bladder is unremarkable.
Normal small and large bowel caliber. No free intraperitoneal fluid.

bank.title: PART 1: KEY CRITERIA REPORTED

subs.title: How it's reported
items: Dedicated Pylorus / Upper GI Section: Positioned right after the liver and gallbladder survey.

subs.title: Key Criteria Reported (Diagnostic Thresholds)
items: Muscle Thickness: Pyloric muscle wall thickness (greater than 3 mm).
Pyloric Channel Length: Longitudinal measurement (greater than 14 to 15 mm).

Morphology: Elongated, thickened pyloric muscle ("cervix sign" or "target sign" on transverse views) with a narrowed, elongated fluid-filled pyloric canal demonstrating absent or sluggish antegrade gastric emptying and vigorous hyperperistalsis of the stomach ("caterpillar sign").

subs.title: Sample Finding Block
items: Pylorus & Upper Gastrointestinal: Real-time evaluation of the pylorus demonstrates marked muscular hypertrophy. The pyloric muscle wall thickness measures [X.X] mm (normal < 3 mm) and the pyloric channel length measures [X.X] mm (normal < 14 mm). The pylorus appears elongated and prominent, creating a classic "cervix sign" with failure of gastric outlet opening and no antegrade passage of gastric contents during real-time observation.
Pyloric stenosis is an epigastric/right upper quadrant evaluation performed primarily in infants presenting with non-bilious projectile vomiting.

bank.title: PART 2: MODULAR DIAGNOSTIC PHRASE BANK — PYLORIC STENOSIS

subs.title: Normal Pylorus (Diagnostic Rule-Out)
items: The pyloric muscle wall thickness measures [X.X] mm (normal less than 3.0 mm) and the pyloric channel length measures [X.X] mm (normal less than 14.0 mm). The pyloric sphincter opens normally with real-time visualization of gastric contents passing freely into the duodenum.

subs.title: Positive Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis (Classic)
items: There is marked concentric thickening of the hypoechoic pyloric muscular layer measuring [X.X] mm (greater than 3.0 mm) and elongation of the pyloric canal measuring [X.X] mm (greater than 14.0 mm), demonstrating classic "cervix" and "target" signs with failure of channel relaxation and no antegrade gastric emptying.

subs.title: Borderline / Developing Pyloric Stenosis (2.5–2.9 mm)
items: The pyloric muscle wall thickness is borderline at [2.7] mm with a channel length of [13.5] mm, demonstrating intermittent, sluggish passage of small amounts of fluid into the duodenum. Findings may represent early/evolving hypertrophic pyloric stenosis or pylorospasm; clinical correlation and repeat ultrasound in 24–48 hours are recommended if vomiting persists.

subs.title: Pylorospasm (Transient Functional Narrowing)
items: Initial transient thickening and elongation of the pyloric canal (measuring up to [3.1] mm) resolved during prolonged real-time observation, with subsequent relaxation of the pyloric muscle to [2.0] mm and normal antegrade passage of gastric fluid into the duodenum, consistent with benign pylorospasm.
